title: Community Update from Mayor Rhodes-Conway (July 31) - City of Madison, WI
text: For Immediate Release July 31, 2026 "There is palpable grief in our community and we must move forward with compassion and grace. I believe Madison can and must do better. A lot better . We need to start that work now. We cannot do that while facing the immediate crisis of an occupation of public spaces. The current blockade of a major thoroughfare detours public bus routes, makes it more difficult for community members to reach their jobs, and impedes fire and EMS response. It is causing real, possibly irreparable, harm to local business owners and community services that remain shut down due to the ongoing occupation.   The people engaging in this activity are members of our community who care about improving Madison and righting legitimate wrongs. But we mustn't squander this energy by abandoning the rule of the law, jeopardizing the livelihoods of our neighbors, and pretending that any single entity, be it City government or someone else, alone, can solve systemic problems overnight. What's currently happening cannot be sustained — in fact, we are wasting precious resources that we need to solve real problems.   The occupation at the intersection of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street must end. Outreach workers are actively connecting unhoused individuals with services and shelter. There are many opportunities to provide mutual aid to people experiencing homelessness, and I encourage everyone to work with organizations already providing that support. This work can often take time and can be complicated, but we are doing our absolute best to find solutions. What remains true is that this intersection is not a safe location for people to be sleeping in tents, nor for children to play alongside nail-studded blockades.  The life of Corey Ruiz will never be forgotten. The intersection of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street will never be the same. I'm committed to realizing a positive vision in collaboration with Corey's family for a memorial in that space so that our community will never forget. Madison needs more hard conversations, and more hard work, to realize a better future. We must take the first step towards having those conversations in a realistic, non-destructive way. And that starts with voluntarily taking down the barricades, coming together to decide what comes next, and channeling our collective momentum towards a better Madison. I stand ready to work on the next phase. It's time for the barricades to come down." — Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway  Subscribe to the City of Madison News Releases email list. title: EXCLUSIVE: Encampment could cost city ‘hundreds of thousands of dollars,’ mayor says - Channel 3000
text: A full interview with Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway will air Sunday on For the Record. MADISON, Wis. — The encampment at the site where a Madison police officer shot and killed a man could cost the city “hundreds of thousands of dollars,” Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway told News 3 Now on Friday. The encampment at the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin streets was erected late last week in response to the killing of Corey Ruiz. Police said Ruiz was seen “checking vehicles” before his encounter with police and used a knife to injure one of the officers detaining him before the shooting. The City of Madison has provided some resources to keep the protest area safe, including salt trucks parked in front of makeshift barricades. Speaking to News 3 Now, Rhodes-Conway said the trucks were put in place to prevent vehicles from crashing through the barricades and injuring people. “Normally when we would have a protest, or something like this, we would have [police] squad cars down to make sure people were staying safe,” Rhodes-Conway said. “Given the sensitivity of this moment, we’ve chosen to use other city staff and vehicles to do that.” EXCLUSIVE: "I would expect just roughly that we are talking about hundreds of thousands of dollars..." Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway addresses the financial impact of the encampment in her first TV interview since an MPD officer shot and killed a man last week. @WISCTV_News3 pic.twitter.com/WaHbeK9uX4 But utilizing city resources that way can only go on for so long. And for some in the area, the encampment is taking a toll on their patience. Rhodes-Conway issued a statement Thursday calling the encampment neither sustainable nor safe. She said residents in the Marquette neighborhood had reached out to her office with concerns about being unable to sleep, conduct business or safely be in the area. The city is also racking up a massive bill, mostly on overtime and staffing costs, that could have impacts further down the line. “I would expect just roughly that we are talking about hundreds of thousands of dollars,” Rhodes-Conway said. She could not provide an exact number on Friday, but said the total would depend on how long the encampment remains up. She said that the city could be forced to amend its budget due to the spending, but could not yet say what other areas would miss out on funding because of the changes. Madison’s budget is already in a tight spot. The city is already projecting an $11 million gap in its 2027 operating budget, and last month Rhodes-Conway directed all city agencies to cut their budgets by 2%. ​COPYRIGHT 2026 BY CHANNEL 3000. title: Businesses, organizations support Madison community after Corey Ruiz shooting - Spectrum News
text: MADISON, Wis. —  As Madison waits for more information in the investigation into the death of Corey Ruiz, protesters continue to gather at the corner of Williamson and Baldwin streets. In the meantime, local businesses and organizations say they are trying to support the community as people process grief, anger and uncertainty. Videos and images of Ruiz’s death spread widely online in the days after the shooting, adding to the emotional toll for many in the community. Precious Adebayo of the Boys & Girls Clubs of Dane County said the young people she works with have been deeply affected. “They have definitely voiced a lot of feeling unsafe by the people that they feel that they are supposed to reach out for, in order for them to feel safe,” Adebayo said. Adebayo said she and other leaders took a group of teens to the memorial at Williamson and Baldwin, as well as to protests, after they expressed interest in participating. She said it was important to give them a space to process what they were feeling and to advocate for their community. “They want to be heard. They want to be more of an advocate,” she said. Adebayo said the Boys & Girls Club is continuing to serve as a safe space for youth as more information about the shooting becomes public. She also encouraged parents and guardians to give teens room to express themselves. “We want to be able to allow them to share what their feedback is of the situation, let them know that their voices matter and that we are not just listening, but they are heard as well,” Adebayo said. Businesses in the area are also adjusting in response to the aftermath of the shooting. The Madison Public Market had planned to hold its grand opening the day after the shooting, but leaders decided to stay closed after consulting with vendors. “With their guidance, we decided to close in honor and respect for what was happening in the community,” said Keisha Harrison, CEO of the Madison Public Market Foundation. The market later held a quieter opening on Wednesday, with a larger celebration planned for a later date. Harrison said she hopes the space can serve as a place for people to gather, reflect and support local businesses during a difficult time. “What we’re hoping is that people will gravitate towards us to come and have some respite, to have a good time, to have that time for reflection,” Harrison said. In a statement Friday, Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said "There is palpable grief in our community and we must move forward with compassion and grace. I believe Madison can and must do better. A lot better. We need to start that work now. We cannot do that while facing the immediate crisis of an occupation of public spaces. The current blockade of a major thoroughfare detours public bus routes, makes it more difficult for community members to reach their jobs, and impedes fire and EMS response. It is causing real, possibly irreparable, harm to local business owners and community services that remain shut down due to the ongoing occupation.” “The occupation at the intersection of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street must end. Outreach workers are actively connecting unhoused individuals with services and shelter. There are many opportunities to provide mutual aid to people experiencing homelessness, and I encourage everyone to work with organizations already providing that support.” Read the full statement here.

title: Madison police shooting ; mayor says protest site  not sustainable or safe
text: Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway issued a statement on Thursday addressing concerns regarding an encampment established to protest the fatal police shooting of Corey Ruiz. MADISON, Wis. - Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway issued a statement on Thursday addressing concerns regarding an encampment established to protest the fatal police shooting of Corey Ruiz. The mayor called the situation at Williamson and Baldwin streets "not sustainable or safe." "What's happening at the intersection of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street is not sustainable or safe. There are a number of immediate public safety and public health concerns that must not be ignored.  There are not enough bathrooms to support the number of people gathering in that area. There is all-day food preparation taking place without refrigeration, sinks, and other basics. Any time a street is blocked, it can impede fire and EMS response to our community. The middle of city streets is not a safe location for people to be sleeping in tents. Yesterday, a person confronted protesters, started cursing at a large crowd, and pushed people. We have received multiple complaints about people being threatened, from both protesters and neighbors.  We are also hearing from Marquette neighborhood residents that they can't sleep, can't conduct business, are experiencing financial hardships, and can't safely move around the neighborhood. Those who also want real change after the police shooting of Corey Ruiz are increasingly failing to understand and losing patience with a protest tactic that seems misaligned with bringing the community together.  Our first priority needs to be the health and safety of our entire community, and I am asking our entire community to take this seriously and be a part of the solution.   City staff, local elected officials, and neighborhood leaders are continuing to connect with residents and local businesses to address ongoing concerns in the Marquette neighborhood. This work is ongoing and takes many forms. The goal remains to engage residents, community organizers, and the business community to work on a path that prioritizes safety, action, and remembering Corey Ruiz. The City of Madison has published a  FAQ page  to address the common inquiries we have been receiving. We will be updating this page regularly.  The City is also aware of misinformation, rumors, and other falsehoods circulating online and in other venues. Please be careful about sharing information that's not from official sources.  Please reach out if you need help – we all need to take care of ourselves in traumatic times.   The 988 Lifeline is available for immediate support. You can also text HOME or HOLA to 741741 to reach a live crisis counselor.  Public Health Madison Dane County has additional resources   (external) , as well."  Related article Madison police shooting: Department lacks bodycams, stirs debate Wisconsin's largest police departments have body cameras except one – Madison. A new debate erupts over why the city doesn’t have them after last week’s fatal police shooting of Corey Ruiz. The backstory: Madison Police Chief John Patterson said officers responded to calls about a man stealing bicycles and checking car doors and confronted him on July 22, but he rode away on a bicycle. FREE DOWNLOAD: Get breaking news alerts in the FOX LOCAL Mobile app for iOS or Android Police later encountered the man again, at Baldwin and Williamson, and the man "fell or was pulled off the bicycle." There was a struggle in the middle of the intersection, and police said the man pulled out a knife and injured an officer. Officers used a taser to try to take the man into custody before the injured officer shot the man, since identified as Ruiz. Ruiz was pronounced dead at a hospital. Madison police said the four involved officers were placed on administrative leave as the Wisconsin Department of Justice Division of Criminal Investigation investigates the shooting as a homicide .  The Madison Police Department does not have body-worn cameras for officers. After prior efforts to fund bodycams were shut down, Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said this week that she will include funding for them in her next budget. title: Mayor asks protesters to remove barricades, leave Madison intersection - WKOW
text: Waiting to see if Mayor will honor interview request MADISON (WKOW) -- It has now been eight days since Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway answered questions from 27 News about the city's response to the shooting and the ongoing encampment near Williamson Street and Baldwin Street. 27 News requested another interview with the mayor again Friday. A city spokesperson asked for information about the topics, format and expected length of the interview. We are still waiting to hear whether the mayor will grant the request. The mayor released a written statement Thursday, but it did not address several questions from 27 News, including how long the city will allow the encampment to remain in place. In a new statement Friday, Rhodes-Conway said the encampment is disrupting bus routes, making it more difficult for people to reach their jobs and limiting fire and EMS response. The mayor is asking people to voluntarily leave the intersection and remove the barricades. She said the occupation of public space cannot continue, while also acknowledging the grief in the community and calling for a path forward. Rhodes-Conway did not provide a timeline for removing the encampment or explain what action the city would take if people do not leave voluntarily. Rhodes-Conway's full statement is below and can also be read here : "There is palpable grief in our community and we must move forward with compassion and grace. I believe Madison can and must do better. A lot better. We need to start that work now. We cannot do that while facing the immediate crisis of an occupation of public spaces. The current blockade of a major thoroughfare detours public bus routes, makes it more difficult for community members to reach their jobs, and impedes fire and EMS response. It is causing real, possibly irreparable, harm to local business owners and community services that remain shut down due to the ongoing occupation. The people engaging in this activity are members of our community who care about improving Madison and righting legitimate wrongs. But we mustn't squander this energy by abandoning the rule of the law, jeopardizing the livelihoods of our neighbors, and pretending that any single entity, be it City government or someone else, alone, can solve systemic problems overnight. What's currently happening cannot be sustained — in fact, we are wasting precious resources that we need to solve real problems. The occupation at the intersection of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street must end. Outreach workers are actively connecting unhoused individuals with services and shelter. There are many opportunities to provide mutual aid to people experiencing homelessness, and I encourage everyone to work with organizations already providing that support. This work can often take time and can be complicated, but we are doing our absolute best to find solutions. What remains true is that this intersection is not a safe location for people to be sleeping in tents, nor for children to play alongside nail-studded blockades. The life of Corey Ruiz will never be forgotten. The intersection of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street will never be the same. I'm committed to realizing a positive vision in collaboration with Corey's family for a memorial in that space so that our community will never forget. Madison needs more hard conversations, and more hard work, to realize a better future. We must take the first step towards having those conversations in a realistic, non-destructive way. And that starts with voluntarily taking down the barricades, coming together to decide what comes next, and channeling our collective momentum towards a better Madison. I stand ready to work on the next phase. It's time for the barricades to come down."

title: Community Update from Mayor Rhodes-Conway (August 1) - City of Madison, WI
text: For Immediate Release  August 1, 2026  "The City of Madison is preparing for a respectful transition at Williamson Street and Baldwin Street. Many in the community are asking for artwork and memorial items at the site to be preserved, and the City intends to honor those requests while working with Corey's family and the broader community on a long-term plan for a memorial.   The Wisconsin Department of Justice's Criminal Division Investigation (DCI) is independently investigating the death of Corey Ruiz. The Madison Police Department is fully cooperating but not in charge of the investigation. It cannot make any arrest decisions pertaining to this investigation and cannot make recommendations for any charges. That authority rests with the Wisconsin Department of Justice and the Dane County District Attorney.  There will be many opportunities — involving multiple government entities — in the days and weeks ahead for people to engage in and advocate for change in our criminal justice system. The City remains committed to creating opportunities to talk about and make changes to policies and programs that are under the City's jurisdiction. There are opportunities to make change at the state level as well. There are many existing nonprofits, faith groups, and networks working to advocate for criminal justice, policing reform, and alternative emergency response systems. We encourage people to engage with them.   The group gathering at the intersection is increasingly made up of people who are experiencing homelessness. The grassroots energy to support our unhoused community is also present, but it needs to be directed toward bolstering existing services — not undermining those efforts. The City and the County have worked hard for years to improve services to those experiencing homelessness. There are many nonprofits and groups that support the unhoused community, provide substance abuse and mental health treatment, and advocate for better services and more housing. Our entire community should be rallying around the soon-to-be-opened Bartillon men's shelter with our people-power and pocketbooks. This first-of-its-kind, purpose-built shelter is currently a partnership between Dane County, the City of Madison, Porchlight, and Shelter Friends of Dane County. It can be an anchor for services for the unhoused community, with your support.  What remains true is that the occupation of the intersection is neither a safe nor a sustainable solution for the unhoused or the surrounding community. It cannot make the independent investigation move faster or change state law. At this point, it is distracting rather than supporting the dialogue and organizing that need to happen to make lasting change. And it is deeply harming the Marquette neighborhood. title: Mayor Rhodes-Conway calls for barricades at Williamson and Baldwin to come down - WKOW
text: MADISON, Wis. — The City of Madison is preparing to reopen the intersection at Williamson Street and Baldwin Street while preserving memorial items for Corey Ruiz. Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said the city plans to work with Ruiz's family and the community on a long-term memorial plan. She said many community members have asked for artwork and memorial items at the site to be preserved, and the city intends to honor those requests. The Wisconsin Department of Justice's Criminal Division Investigation is independently investigating Ruiz's death. The Madison Police Department is fully cooperating but is not in charge of the investigation and cannot make arrest decisions or recommend charges. Rhodes-Conway said that authority rests with the Wisconsin Department of Justice and the Dane County District Attorney. The mayor said there will be many opportunities in the coming days and weeks for people to engage in and advocate for changes in the criminal justice system. She said the city remains committed to creating opportunities to discuss and make changes to policies and programs under the city's jurisdiction. Rhodes-Conway said the group gathering at the intersection is increasingly made up of people experiencing homelessness. She said grassroots energy to support the unhoused community needs to be directed toward bolstering existing services rather than undermining those efforts. "The City and the County have worked hard for years to improve services to those experiencing homelessness," Rhodes-Conway said. "There are many nonprofits and groups that support the unhoused community, provide substance abuse and mental health treatment, and advocate for better services and more housing." The mayor called on the community to support the soon-to-be-opened Bartillon men's shelter. She said the first-of-its-kind, purpose-built shelter is a partnership between Dane County, the City of Madison, Porchlight and Friends of Dane County Shelter. Rhodes-Conway said the occupation of the intersection is neither safe nor sustainable for the unhoused or the surrounding community. She said it cannot make the independent investigation move faster or change state law. "At this point, it is distracting rather than supporting the dialogue and organizing that need to happen to make lasting change," Rhodes-Conway said. "And it is deeply harming the Marquette neighborhood." The mayor said barricades must come down, people need to access their homes and jobs, and businesses need to be able to open. She said the city's goal of a respectful transition can be accomplished if people on the ground take action. Rhodes-Conway said barricades need to be deconstructed, vehicles obstructing the right-of-way need to be moved, and tents need to come down. She said the vigil site and other memorial items need to be preserved or situated to allow for a new traffic pattern. The city stands ready to work with anyone on the site willing to act now to move forward.

title: Community Update from Mayor Rhodes-Conway (August 2) - City of Madison, WI
text: For Immediate Release August 2, 2026 “I want to thank the Madison community for their patience as we work to reopen the intersection of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street, while also ensuring that those who want to visit a memorial will have space to do so. City of Madison staff and community partners have been actively delivering the message that the best path forward is for the occupation to end peacefully so the real work of healing the community and enacting change can begin.   There is real harm being done to local businesses and residents in the Marquette Neighborhood. We are hearing from neighbors who are losing income and even jobs, and who will not be able to make rent. We are hearing from employees who are being laid off and businesses that are on the verge of closing permanently. Those who are dismissing or downplaying these concerns are not helping to advance a just cause; they are dividing our city at a time when we need to come together more than ever.   The group gathering at the intersection is increasingly made up of people who are experiencing homelessness. In the past week, local elected officials, City staff, and partners have taken numerous steps to help facilitate a smooth and peaceful transition of this space. The Dane County Behavioral Resource Center and other mental health organizations have provided crisis counseling on site. Every day, the City's Community Development Division has worked closely with City-contracted street outreach agencies and others on site to identify and connect with vulnerable unsheltered persons. City resources have been made available to the agencies to allow them to secure short-term hotel accommodations for about 25-30 people, including 4-5 families with children. Some people have declined those offers. This weekend, staff have delivered meals to folks in hotels and are coordinating with community groups to ensure that meals continue to be delivered. This is work that the City does year round to support people experiencing homelessness – to learn more about that work please visit this site .   What the City has NOT done is to supply porta-potties, dumpsters, or financial support to the occupation effort. Any assertions to the contrary are false and are among the many rumors and misinformation circulating online.   There are simple next steps that will ensure a peaceful and collaborative end to the occupation:  As a city and country, we have much more work to do in addressing the systemic issues highlighted by this occupation — but it is also important to recognize that we have a foundation to build on in our community. In the past few years, Madison has launched and expanded an alternative to police calls through the CARES program. We've added hundreds of homes through social housing and helped build thousands of affordable homes through the private market, and will continue to do so in the upcoming years. Through our partnership with Dane County, Madison is making historic investments in homeless services and opening the very first purpose-built men's shelter in Wisconsin. Madison pioneered community policing and now we need to perfect community oversight of the police, while also acknowledging the constraints placed on local communities by the state. The City has worked and will work cooperatively with individuals, nonprofits, the faith community, and anyone who is acting in good faith to ensure a peaceful resolution is reached, and reached soon.   But I want to make it very clear: the occupation of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street needs to end now."  — Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway  Subscribe to the City of Madison News Releases email list. title: Letter | The silence is getting loud - The Cap Times
text: Dear Editor: I’m not a lifelong local, but I’m a resident who pays attention. I walk this city, pay my taxes, and listen to the tone of the people around me. Lately, that tone feels muted. Not angry, not dramatic — just quiet. Almost like Madison is speaking in a lower register than it used to. Under Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway, the city has taken on a more subdued vibe. She’s done good things — that’s clear, but her public presence feels understated. Reserved. The kind of leadership that stays behind the curtain instead of stepping into the spotlight. In bigger cities, mayors are part of the daily rhythm. Press conferences, announcements, community events and reminders that someone is steering the ship. Madison doesn’t have that right now. While charisma isn’t required for good leadership, visibility matters more than people admit. It’s not about showmanship; it’s about connection. I met the mayor once. She was kind, and I appreciated it. Kindness in a moment doesn’t replace presence over time. As taxes rise and frustrations simmer, I hear people speaking in low tones. Not outrage, but fatigue, a quiet call for reassurance. Madison feels different since the Soglin days. It’s not better or worse — just different. Soglin was loud and present. Today, the city’s rhythm feels more like a John Klemmer sax solo: atmospheric, introspective, almost too subtle for the moment we’re in. Rodney Jenkins Madison

title: Madison police shooting; mayor says protest site 'not sustainable or safe' - AOL.com
text: 0 The Brief Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway addressed concerns Thursday about an encampment protesting the fatal police shooting of Corey Ruiz. Conditions at Williamson and Baldwin streets are "not sustainable or safe," the mayor stated. There's no word on if the city plans to take any action to clear the area. MADISON, Wis. - Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway issued a statement on Thursday addressing concerns regarding an encampment established to protest the fatal police shooting of Corey Ruiz. The mayor called the situation at Williamson and Baldwin streets "not sustainable or safe." "What's happening at the intersection of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street is not sustainable or safe. There are a number of immediate public safety and public health concerns that must not be ignored. There are not enough bathrooms to support the number of people gathering in that area. There is all-day food preparation taking place without refrigeration, sinks, and other basics. Any time a street is blocked, it can impede fire and EMS response to our community. The middle of city streets is not a safe location for people to be sleeping in tents. Yesterday, a person confronted protesters, started cursing at a large crowd, and pushed people. We have received multiple complaints about people being threatened, from both protesters and neighbors. We are also hearing from Marquette neighborhood residents that they can't sleep, can't conduct business, are experiencing financial hardships, and can't safely move around the neighborhood. Those who also want real change after the police shooting of Corey Ruiz are increasingly failing to understand and losing patience with a protest tactic that seems misaligned with bringing the community together. Our first priority needs to be the health and safety of our entire community, and I am asking our entire community to take this seriously and be a part of the solution. City staff, local elected officials, and neighborhood leaders are continuing to connect with residents and local businesses to address ongoing concerns in the Marquette neighborhood. This work is ongoing and takes many forms. The goal remains to engage residents, community organizers, and the business community to work on a path that prioritizes safety, action, and remembering Corey Ruiz. The City of Madison has published a FAQ page to address the common inquiries we have been receiving. We will be updating this page regularly. The City is also aware of misinformation, rumors, and other falsehoods circulating online and in other venues. Please be careful about sharing information that's not from official sources. Advertisement Please reach out if you need help – we all need to take care of ourselves in traumatic times. The 988 Lifeline is available for immediate support. You can also text HOME or HOLA to 741741 to reach a live crisis counselor. Public Health Madison Dane County has additional resources (external) , as well." The backstory Madison Police Chief John Patterson said officers responded to calls about a man stealing bicycles and checking car doors and confronted him on July 22, but he rode away on a bicycle. FREE DOWNLOAD: Get breaking news alerts in the FOX LOCAL Mobile app for iOS or Android Police later encountered the man again, at Baldwin and Williamson, and the man "fell or was pulled off the bicycle." There was a struggle in the middle of the intersection, and police said the man pulled out a knife and injured an officer. Officers used a taser to try to take the man into custody before the injured officer shot the man, since identified as Ruiz. Ruiz was pronounced dead at a hospital. Madison police said the four involved officers were placed on administrative leave as the Wisconsin Department of Justice Division of Criminal Investigation investigates the shooting as a homicide . The Madison Police Department does not have body-worn cameras for officers. After prior efforts to fund bodycams were shut down, Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said this week that she will include funding for them in her next budget. The Source The information in this post was provided by Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway, the Madison Police Department, Wisconsin Department of Justice, Madison Police Civilian Oversight Board.
